The Black-billed cuckoo (Coccyzus erythropthalmus) is a medium-sized, relatively secretive Neotropical migrant that breeds across the eastern deciduous forests of North America. During the early stages of development, the freshly laid egg mass, referred to as the initial wet weight, has been measured at 6.3 grams [Ww0 = 6.3 grams], a value characteristic of the genus. Upon pipping and emergence, the wet weight at birth of a newly hatched nestling is approximately 7.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 7.5 grams], reflecting the substantial yolk reserves allocated to the altricial chick. This impressive postnatal mass gain continues rapidly, with the ultimate wet weight for adult females reaching 48.5 grams [Wwi = 48.5 grams], while males, exhibiting a slight sexual size dimorphism, attain a lower adult body mass of 45.8 grams [Wwi = 45.8 grams]. These mass values are consistent with the species’ reliance on relatively large, soft-bodied prey such as caterpillars and katydids, which facilitate rapid chick provisioning.

Incubation in the Black-billed cuckoo is initiated with the first egg, and the resulting asynchronous hatching creates considerable variation in nestling age within a single brood. Eggs held at a constant incubator temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C] require a mean incubation period of approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] before pipping commences, although under natural nest conditions the pre-hatching interval can range from 10 to 13 days depending on ambient thermal regimes. This relatively brief embryonic development is typical of the Cuculidae and may be an adaptation that reduces exposure to nest predators during the conspicuous nesting phase. Once hatched, the altricial nestlings grow rapidly, achieving adult mass within a few weeks, and the species exhibits a single annual brood in most parts of its range, with the potential for a second clutch following early nest success.

Under the metabolically active thermal conditions typical of the cuckoo's breeding season, maintained at approximately 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a predictable sequence of juvenile milestones unfolds. The time since birth at fledging, marking the age at which the young achieve sustained flight and depart the nest, is estimated at 21 days [tx = 21 days] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. It is important to note that the fledging period can sometimes be as brief as 7 to 9 days [tx = 7 to 9 days] in cases of nest disturbance, but the typical, undisturbed duration is the three-week interval (21 days) [tx = 21 days] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Following nest departure, the fledglings remain dependent on their parents for food for an additional two to three weeks, gradually honing their foraging skills on a diet of caterpillars and other insects before attaining full independence. This post-fledging dependency period is critical for developing the muscular coordination necessary for effective aerial hawking.

The species’ life history is further characterized by a relatively rapid maturation schedule. The time since birth at puberty, representing the onset of gonadal activity and the acquisition of adult plumage characteristics, occurs at 63 days [tp = 63 days] under the same ecologically relevant body temperature of the breeding season at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This early sexual maturity is relatively swift compared to many other migratory birds of similar body size, allowing first-year birds to potentially join the breeding population in the spring following their hatching year. The first successful reproduction event, however, is typically deferred until the following summer. Reproductive output in the Black-billed cuckoo is modest, yet well-suited to its strategy of placing a single, well-provisioned brood within a resource-rich season. Females lay between 2 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 to 4 eggs per clutch], a relatively small clutch size for an insectivorous bird of its mass, and typically produce only 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year]. The maximum longevity recorded for this species in the wild is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years], a figure that reflects the cumulative risks of migration, predation on the nest, and the stochastic availability of its preferred caterpillar prey during the breeding season at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This lifespan, combined with its annual reproductive effort, suggests that a productive individual may contribute only a handful of recruits to the population over its lifetime, underscoring the importance of high juvenile survival during the post-fledging and migratory phases.
